USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep List 1 in force and let the already-scheduled List 2 duties proceed on 23 August, but do not implement List 3 or raise its proposed rate to 25% while the comment/hearing process is still open. Reopen a narrow negotiating channel now, conditioned on structural IP/tech-transfer remedies rather than another purchase-only communiqué. Use the $200B list as leverage on the table, not as an automatic next shot.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly negative (an opportunity, not a danger) because the US macro backdrop is still strong while China is absorbing more of the shock: industrial production is up to 104.0, VIX is 14.64, and the dollar has firmed ~7%, while US goods exports to China have already fallen ~27% and the yuan has weakened to 6.93 (about +9.4% USD/CNY in the window), which both hurts US farm exporters and partly offsets the tariff wedge. The Section 301 finding of 22 March and the collapse of the 19 May “trade war on hold” joint statement show China will offer purchases, not IP reform; that is leverage, not an existential threat. Action should stay near zero because a further jump to 25% on ~$200B (directed 1 August; hearings 20–23 August) would hit consumer-facing lines the first lists deliberately spared, invite China’s threatened $60B counter-list, and deepen soybean/farm-belt damage already running ~20% on prices after the 6 July matching $34B retaliation. ZTE was already spent and then walked back (ban lifted 13 July for $1.4B), so another non-tariff lunge would look inconsistent. Hold the existing tariffs, finish the List 3 record, and negotiate from that position.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer case remains unmet after the May truce collapsed
List 1 ($34B at 25%) is live with dollar-for-dollar Chinese retaliation; List 2 is queued for 23 August
List 3 ($200B) is still in comment/hearing; raising it to 25% is proposed, not decided
US real economy still firm (IP, low VIX) while bilateral US exports to China are down ~27% and the goods deficit has widened
Yuan depreciation to ~6.93 and farm-belt soybean price drop (~20%) are the main US costs and also erode tariff bite
ZTE denial-order leverage was already used and then lifted in July

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines). Public comment / hearing process begins.
At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
US exports of goods to mainland China fell from $12.65B (2018-03) to $9.28B (2018-08), about -26.7% over the window.
US imports from China rose from $38.3B (2018-03) to $47.8B (2018-08), about +24.9%, consistent with front-loading ahead of further tariffs.
CNY per USD rose from ~6.34 in late February to 6.933 on 2018-08-15 (+9.4%), a material offset to US tariff incidence.
US industrial production index 104.03 on 2018-08-01, up ~1.8% in the window — no recession signal from the dispute yet.
VIX 14.64 on 2018-08-15, down from ~20.6 in February; markets are not pricing a systemic US shock.
Michigan consumer sentiment slipped from 101.4 (March) to 96.2 (August), a soft domestic-confidence cost.
Ohio soybean farmer: ~20% price drop; USDA crop report sent futures down >4.5% on 10 August; China was the No. 1 customer.
Nearly one-third of US soybeans (~$14B) go to China; 25% Chinese duty on 545 US items (soy, pork, dairy, etc.) targets Trump-country ag.
After the 1 August 10%→25% instruction, List 3 hearings still start 20 August; written comments extended to 5 September.
List 2 duties set for 23 August; China said it will add tariffs on another ~$60B of US goods if the US proceeds with the $200B third round.
Commerce lifted the ZTE denial order on 13 July after a $1B penalty plus $400M escrow — the main non-tariff lever was already spent.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture. Keep in force the July 6 matching tariffs and the already-announced August $16B match, and leave the August 3 $60B list strictly contingent on a U.S. List 3 implementation. Do not add new tariff or non-tariff measures while List 3 is still in the comment window, do not re-table a large purchase package after the May truce collapsed, and quietly stabilize the yuan enough to avoid handing Washington a pretext to lift List 3 from 10% to 25%.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. The live hit is still the $34B List 1 (in force since 2018-07-06) plus the imminent $16B List 2, while the real damage risk is the proposed ~$200B List 3, which USTR published on 2018-07-10 and, on 2018-08-01, said it is considering raising from 10% to 25%. That would take U.S. coverage far beyond what China can match dollar-for-dollar (2017 U.S. goods imports were about $154B; after $50B already committed, the August 3 $60B list already stretches remaining import ammunition). The April 16 ZTE denial order showed Washington can shut a national champion via the entity/denial channel even though the ban was lifted on 2018-07-13 after a $1B fine and $400M escrow. FX pressure is already material: DEXCHUS moved from about 6.33 in late February to 6.933 on 2018-08-15 (~9.4%), and the broad dollar is up ~7%; contemporaneous coverage treated the slide as a possible U.S. trigger for a 25% List 3 rate. That combination sits near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors hit, FX pressure, firm-level targeting) but below it because industrial production is still ~6.1% y/y, merchandise exports have not collapsed, reserves are only ~1% lower, and List 3 is not yet in force. Action should stay at hold, not escalate or concede. Further tariff escalation now would likely raise the odds the U.S. implements List 3 at 25% and would exhaust remaining U.S. import targets without changing U.S. leverage. Re-offering purchases or a rollback would repeat the 2018-05-19 joint statement that the White House discarded on 2018-05-29. The disciplined stance is to keep the $60B list as a credible contingent answer, refuse structural IP/Made-in-2025 giveaways while talks are dead, and use the List 3 comment period to prepare export diversion and yuan-stability measures rather than fire unused tools.
key_factors: Proposed $200B List 3, with USTR considering a hike from 10% to 25% (2018-07-10 / 2018-08-01)
Asymmetric remaining tariff ammunition: China already matched $50B and can only threaten ~$60B more
CNY depreciation of ~9% since February and a stronger dollar, read in the U.S. as a possible offset to tariffs
ZTE denial order demonstrated lethal non-tariff leverage even though the ban was later lifted on costly terms
May 19 purchase-truce collapsed within ten days; unilateral concessions are not reciprocated
China real-side data still holding (IP ~6%, exports not collapsing), so the threat is prospective more than realized

At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.

White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.

Goldman: decision to raise List 3 from 10% to 25% may depend in part on whether recent CNY depreciation reverses or continues.
On 2018-08-08 China matched the U.S. $16B List 2 with 25% duties (coal, crude, autos, etc.), effective with the U.S. list on Aug. 23.
